chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Working Capital Really Is

lessons.title: Current Assets and Current Liabilities: Reading the Working Capital Lines on a Balance Sheet

children.text: Every number you will use in this course comes from two blocks of a balance sheet: current assets and current liabilities. If you cannot find them and read them line by line, working capital stays an abstract idea. So this lesson does one thing well. It takes an Indian balance sheet extract apart, line by line, and shows you what each line is really telling you about the cash inside the business.
Indian companies present these lines in a fixed order set by
of the Companies Act, 2013. Once you know that order, every annual report in the country looks the same.

markDefs.definition: The format the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes for every Indian company's balance sheet and profit and loss statement, including the split between current and non-current items.

children.text: The Test: What Makes an Item Current?
An asset is current if the business expects to convert it into cash, sell it or consume it within 12 months, or within its

if that cycle is longer. It is also current if it is cash, or if it is held mainly for trading. A liability is current if it falls due within 12 months or within the operating cycle, or if the company has no unconditional right to defer it beyond 12 months. Everything else is non-current.

markDefs.definition: The time between buying raw material and collecting cash from the customer for the goods made from it. Where this exceeds 12 months, it, and not 12 months, decides what counts as current.

columns.label: Current
points: Steel lying in the stores, expected to be used this quarter
An invoice raised on a customer, payable in 60 days
The cash credit balance the bank can recall on demand
The next four quarterly instalments of a term loan
GST payable for March, due in April

columns.label: Non-current
points: The factory building and the machines inside it
A security deposit with the electricity board, refundable after five years
The part of a five-year term loan due after March next year
Investment in a subsidiary held for the long term

body.text: Notice that one loan can sit in both blocks. A five-year term loan is split: instalments due in the next 12 months are current, the rest is non-current. This single split trips up more first-time readers than any other line on the balance sheet.

body.title: When 12 months is the wrong test

children.text: Schedule III lets the operating cycle override the 12-month rule when that cycle is longer. A real estate developer building a tower over four years, a shipbuilder, or a heavy engineering firm executing multi-year projects will classify inventory and receivables tied to those projects as current, even though the cash is years away.

So when you read a balance sheet, check the accounting policy note for the company's stated operating cycle before you assume that "current" means "within a year". Two companies with identical current ratios can be very different if one turns its cycle in 60 days and the other takes four years.

body.title: The classification rule
body.textWithBlank: Under Schedule III, an asset is current if it is expected to be realised within 12 months or within the company's ___ cycle, whichever is longer.
body.explanation: The operating cycle, the time from buying raw material to collecting cash for the finished goods, overrides the 12-month test when it is longer. This is why real estate and shipbuilding balance sheets carry very large current assets.

children.text: Reading the Lines: One Balance Sheet Extract

Below is the current section of the balance sheet of Sunrise Ceramics Ltd, an illustrative mid-sized tile maker in Morbi, Gujarat, for FY2026. The line names and their order follow the Schedule III format you will see in any Indian annual report.

body.caption: Sunrise Ceramics Ltd, current assets as at 31 March 2026 (₹ crore)

cells: Inventories
Clay and glaze, work in progress, finished tiles, packing material and stores
Trade receivables
Invoices raised on dealers and builders, not yet collected
Cash and cash equivalents
Bank current account balances and deposits of up to three months
Other bank balances
Margin money pledged against letters of credit and bank guarantees, so not freely usable
Other financial assets
Interest accrued, security deposits due back within a year, unbilled revenue
Other current assets
GST input credit, advances paid to suppliers, prepaid insurance and rent
Total current assets

body.title: Where Sunrise Ceramics keeps its current assets (₹ crore)

children.text: Two lines, receivables and inventories, make up ₹100 crore of the ₹122 crore total. That is the shape of most manufacturing and trading balance sheets in India, and it tells you immediately where the cash is trapped. Note also that the ₹4 crore of other bank balances is pledged as margin money, so treating it as spendable cash would be a mistake.

body.text: Two lines that look harmless deserve a second look. GST input credit inside other current assets is real money, but only if the business has enough output tax to set it off against. Unbilled revenue inside other financial assets is work already done that the customer has not even been invoiced for yet, so it is one step further from cash than a normal receivable.

body.caption: Sunrise Ceramics Ltd, current liabilities as at 31 March 2026 (₹ crore)

cells: Borrowings: cash credit from bank
The working capital limit, drawn against inventory and receivables
Borrowings: current maturities of long-term debt
Term loan instalments falling due within 12 months
Trade payables: dues to micro and small enterprises
Disclosed separately because of the MSME payment law
Trade payables: dues to others
Larger suppliers, transporters and service vendors
Other financial liabilities
Salaries and bonus payable, unpaid expenses, capital creditors
Other current liabilities
Advances received from dealers, GST and TDS payable
Provisions
Leave encashment, gratuity and warranty amounts due within a year
Total current liabilities

body.label: Working capital of Sunrise Ceramics
body.context: Current assets of ₹122 crore minus current liabilities of ₹101 crore. The current ratio works out to 1.21.

body.title: Compute it yourself
body.prompt: Using the two tables above, what is Sunrise Ceramics' net working capital in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Total current assets of ₹122 crore minus total current liabilities of ₹101 crore gives ₹21 crore. Notice how small that is next to ₹58 crore of receivables: most of the cycle is being funded by the bank and by suppliers.

children.text: The Traps Hiding in These Lines
A balance sheet is a photograph taken on 31 March, not a video of the year. Several lines flatter the picture if you read them without asking the follow-up question.

stats.label: Cash and equivalents
stats.context: But ₹4 crore more sits in pledged margin money that cannot be spent

stats.label: Trade receivables
stats.context: The ageing schedule, not this total, tells you how much is collectible

stats.label: Current maturities
stats.context: A long-term loan repayment that must be funded like any other current bill

children.text: Since the Schedule III amendments effective from 1 April 2021, two of those follow-up questions are much easier to answer. Companies must now publish ageing schedules for both trade receivables and trade payables, bucketed as less than six months, six months to one year, one to two years, two to three years and more than three years. They must also show current maturities of long-term borrowings inside current borrowings rather than buried in other financial liabilities.

body.text: When you open an annual report, go straight to the trade receivables ageing note. A company where 85% of receivables are under six months is running a different business from one where 30% are more than a year old, even if both report the same total.

body.title: Which one is not a current liability?
body.question: A company has the following items on 31 March. Which of them does NOT belong in current liabilities?
options: The outstanding cash credit balance with its bank
A term loan instalment due in four months
The portion of a five-year term loan repayable in years two to five
GST collected in March and payable in April
body.explanation: Only instalments due within the next 12 months are current. The rest of a five-year term loan is a non-current liability. The cash credit balance is repayable on demand, the instalment due in four months is a current maturity, and GST payable in April is due within the year.

body.title: The current ratio that lies
body.scenario: A family-owned business hands you its FY2026 balance sheet. Current assets are ₹122 crore, current liabilities are ₹101 crore, so the current ratio is 1.21 and the owner calls it comfortable. The ageing note then shows ₹11 crore of trade receivables outstanding for more than two years, including two disputed amounts. The inventory note shows ₹6 crore of discontinued tile designs that have not moved in three years.
body.prompt: Restate working capital and the current ratio after treating those two amounts as not realisable, and say what you would ask the owner next.
body.modelAnswer:
Strip both out. Current assets fall from ₹122 crore to ₹105 crore. Working capital falls from ₹21 crore to ₹4 crore, and the current ratio falls from 1.21 to 1.04, which is effectively no cushion at all.

That changes the conversation completely. The business is funding old receivables and dead stock with a bank limit that has to be serviced every month.

What to ask next: are the two disputed receivables in arbitration or litigation, and has any provision been made against them? What is the realisable value of the discontinued designs if sold at a discount or as scrap? How much headroom is left on the cash credit limit? And has the auditor commented on either item? The balance sheet total told you nothing useful. The notes told you everything.

children.text: How to Do This on a Real Annual Report

body.title: Find and read the working capital lines in any Indian annual report
steps: Open the annual report PDF and go to the standalone balance sheet, usually a single page titled "Balance Sheet as at 31 March".
Read the current assets block from inventories down to other current assets, and note the note number printed against each line.
Jump to those notes: the inventory note splits raw material, work in progress and finished goods, and the receivables note carries the ageing schedule.
Read the current liabilities block, separating bank borrowings from trade payables. Check the MSME dues line and the trade payables ageing schedule.
Check the accounting policy note for the stated operating cycle, so you know what "current" means for this company.
Compute current assets minus current liabilities, then recompute it after removing pledged bank balances, old receivables and slow-moving inventory.
Repeat for the previous year printed alongside, so you see the direction of travel and not just one snapshot.

body.label: Screener.in balance sheet view
body.description: Screener compresses the current blocks into "Other Liabilities" and "Other Assets", which is fine for spotting trends but too coarse for line-level work. Use it to see the trend, then open the annual report note for the detail.

body.text: Current assets minus current liabilities is a number anyone can compute. What separates a useful reader from a careless one is knowing which lines inside those totals will actually turn into cash, and when.

children.text: In the next lesson you will meet sharper versions of this number. Notice that if you strip out cash, pledged deposits and all bank borrowing from the two tables above, Sunrise Ceramics is left with ₹53.5 crore of purely operating working capital, more than double the ₹21 crore headline. That gap is the subject of the next lesson.

points: Indian balance sheets follow Schedule III, so current assets and current liabilities appear in the same order in every annual report.
An item is current if it will be realised or settled within 12 months or within the operating cycle, whichever is longer.
Inventories and trade receivables dominate current assets in most manufacturing and trading businesses, which is where working capital is trapped.
Current maturities of long-term debt sit inside current borrowings and must be funded like any other short-term bill.
Pledged margin money, GST input credit and unbilled revenue are current assets but are not the same as spendable cash.
Since the 2021 Schedule III amendments, receivables and payables ageing schedules are published, and they matter far more than the headline totals.
